## Problem

The lab serves fine-tuned or downloaded model artefacts: an HF
checkpoint, a local GGUF, a trained adapter directory. "We think
this came from us last Tuesday" is not a trust statement. Models move
as directories of files; a file-hash in a README is unauthenticated.
The task: an identity-bound, tamper-evident signature over the model
directory. A verifier checks it WITHOUT a key-distribution
ceremony: exactly the Sigstore model-signing flow. The D-4 manifest
row carries it (`modelsign`, wrapping the real
sigstore/model-transparency project — post-os#210 URL correction).

## Solution

Sign with Sigstore keyless (the OIDC identity is the trust anchor), or
with a plain key pair when the box is offline. Verify the same
identity back:

```bash
# 1. Confirm the rows + the CLI surface at your pin
kailash info modelsign        # d-04 row: wraps sigstore/model-transparency

# 2. Sign a model directory, keyless (Sigstore default; opens an OIDC
#    flow — browser or device-code — and records the event to Rekor)
modelsign sign ./path/to/model-dir --signature <model>.sig
#    (the wrapping CLI's shape; sigstore/model-signing's canonical CLI is
#     `model_signing` — the flags it carries below are its verified surface)

# 3. Verify before you USE a downloaded model — identity must be a
#    value you EXPECT (from the trainer's published verification
#    instructions, never "whatever signed it"):
model_signing verify ./path/to/model-dir \
  --signature <model>.sig \
  --identity "<signer-identity>" --identity_provider "<oidc-provider>"
#    -> signature valid + recomputed per-file digests match the bundle's
#       signed subject list

# 4. Negative case (the proof it is doing something): ANY file in the
#    directory changed since signing?
echo x >> ./path/to/model-dir/some-file
model_signing verify ./path/to/model-dir --signature <model>.sig \
  --identity "<signer-identity>" --identity_provider "<oidc-provider>"
#    -> verification FAILS (digest mismatch). Restore the file.

# 5. Offline/lab-closed alternative — plain key pair signing:
openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out key.priv
openssl ec -in key.priv -pubout > key.pub
model_signing sign key ./model-dir --private_key key.priv --signature model.sig
model_signing verify key ./model-dir --signature model.sig --public_key key.pub

# 6. Transparency-log side-quest: WHO signed WHAT, WHEN (the Rekor
#    log itself + cosign's container view for comparison):
cosign verify <registry>/<image>:<tag> \
  --certificate-identity "<identity>" --certificate-oidc-issuer "<issuer>"
#    -> container images verify against the registry; model dirs verify
#       against the local bundle — know which world your artefact is in
```

Expected output shape (abridged):

```
$ model_signing verify ./bert-base-uncased --signature model.sig \
     --identity "user@example.com" --identity_provider "https://github.com/login/oauth"
Verification succeeded.   # signature checks; per-file digests match
$ (file modified)
Verification failed: <file> digest mismatch
```

What success looks like:

- signing produced a signature bundle/JSON file
- the Sigstore bundle carries the DSSE envelope, the certificate, and
  the Rekor inclusion proof — not a bare detached hash
- verification names the PREDICTED identity (not merely "any valid
  chain") and fails on a single-file tamper
- the keyless path's first run opened an OIDC flow
- the key path worked with no network beyond the local box
- model-card metadata that matters to the governance story sits
  inside the signed statement (the predicate carries the metadata
  payload per the upstream format)
- so "who says What about this model" is itself covered

## Discussion

- **Why Sigstore and not "just sign with GPG":** model directories are
  big (multi-GB) and multi-file; hashing is per-file-shard work
  upstream. The model-signing approach gives a per-file digest set
  bound into a DSSE-signed in-toto statement — so the verifier gets
  file-level granularity and identity binding via the OIDC provider
  (Google /
  GitHub / Microsoft / CI workload identities supported upstream), and
  a Transparency-log record of the signing event (verifiers get proof
  of inclusion in Rekor from the bundle itself). Signers should monitor
  the log for unexpected signing events under their identity — that is
  exactly the discovery the transparency log buys.
- **Where the kailash row stands:** the manifest row `modelsign` pins
  sigstore/model-signing (Apache-2.0, safety: safe — this is pure
  signature work, no firing, no target). The signature produced by the
  pinned upstream CLI is the format contract. This recipe is
  the canonical check that the packaged wrapper agrees with the
  upstream surface at the lock's pin.
- **Cosign and model_signing are two ends of the same design:** cosign
  covers containers and blobs (signature attached to registry or
  bundle next to file); model_signing covers model directories with
  per-file semantics. A model loaded INTO a container is in both
  worlds — sign the container AND the model directory. The two
  signatures together cover the artefact and its contents.
- **Private Sigstore instances:** labs that run their own Fulcio/Rekor
  (the air-gapped/enterprise shape) pass `--trust_config` on both sign
  and verify. The identity/provider flags still bind the human claim,
  the trust config binds the infrastructure claim. Keep both in the
  SAME story when citing a verification downstream.
- **CI-shaped signing:** an automated pipeline signs with its workload
  identity (GitHub Actions' token identity
  `https://<org>/<repo>/.github/workflows/<wf>.yml@refs/heads/main`
  per the upstream's supported provider list). A verifier can then
  demand exactly that identity — provenance without a human in the
  loop but with a nameable one.
- **SLSA for models:** sigstore's model-transparency README names the
  SLSA-for-ML extension as the statement's predicate lineage. That
  provenance story ([Prove what an installed artefact
  is](sbom-artifact-verify.html)) and this recipe's signature
  statement share the same in-toto machinery. The two aim at
  different artefact classes. Use both; cite each for what it covers.
